Aged blended rum; flavor and strength vary by bottling.

High-strength Jamaican rum, distinct from standard-strength rum in a recipe.
Demerara rum; choose a bottling and strength to suit the recipe.
Demerara rum; choose a bottle and strength to suit the recipe.

Barrel-aged sugarcane-juice rhum in the agricole style.

Barrel-aged rhum agricole (rhum agricole vieux), distilled from fresh sugarcane juice.
Dark rum for recipes explicitly calling for black rum; bottlings differ substantially.

Gin in the Old Tom style, typically sweeter than dry gin; bottlings vary.
Gin in the Old Tom style, typically sweeter than dry gin; bottles vary.
Plymouth gin for recipes that specify it.

High-strength gin; strength affects the cocktail recipe.

Gin at around 57% ABV, such as Hayman’s Royal Dock. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for London Dry Gin.
Genever for recipes that specify this style.
Malty Dutch and Belgian juniper spirit, the ancestor of gin.
A neutral, unflavored spirit for recipes calling for vodka. Flavored vodkas can be added as distinct ingredients.
Neutral, unflavored vodka, what a recipe means by plain vodka. Flavored vodkas are their own types in this family and don’t fill these recipes.
Tequila, mezcal, and related agave spirits.
Tequila in the blanco style, distinct from barrel-aged tequila in recipes.
Unaged or briefly rested tequila, also called plata.
Barrel-rested tequila in the reposado style.
Tequila rested two to twelve months in oak.
Aged tequila in the añejo style, kept distinct from blanco and reposado.
Tequila aged one to three years in oak.
Mezcal; agave variety and bottling can change the result.
Mezcal; agave variety and bottle can change the result.
French-style grape brandy in common cocktail usage, including Cognac and Armagnac. Apple brandy has a separate family.
Brandy in common cocktail usage: French grape brandy and apple brandy.
French grape brandy from the Cognac region, used in brandy cocktails.
French grape brandy from the Armagnac region; keep distinct when a recipe specifies it.
French grape brandy from Gascony, usually more rustic than cognac.
Apple brandy and applejack styles used in recipes. Decide which types describe your bottles; a broad family reference can use any of these types.
Apple brandy for recipes specifying an apple-based spirit without a narrower style. Classify bottles to suit your recipes.
Regular apple brandy as a recipe ingredient, alongside the separate Bonded Apple Brandy, Applejack, and Calvados types. Use Apple Brandy Family when a recipe permits any of the included styles.

Apple brandy for recipes calling for it without naming a style. Plain apple brandy bottles go here; Bonded Apple Brandy, Applejack, and Calvados are its subtypes, so their bottles fill these recipes too.
Apple brandy for recipes specifying bonded apple brandy, typically at 100 US proof (50% ABV). Assign bottles deliberately; proof alone does not establish bonded status.
Apple brandy for recipes specifying bonded apple brandy, at 100 US proof (50% ABV). Assign bottles deliberately; proof alone does not establish bonded status.
Bottled-in-bond apple brandy at 100 US proof (50% ABV), such as Laird’s Bonded. Not every 100-proof apple brandy is bonded.
Applejack as named in recipes. Bottlings vary; decide which bottles fit the recipe style you intend.
Applejack as named in recipes. Bottles vary; decide which bottles fit the recipe style you intend.
American apple brandy blended with neutral spirit, such as Laird’s Applejack. Older recipes that say applejack often mean any American apple brandy.
Calvados for recipes specifying this apple brandy style. Decide which of your bottles fit the recipe requirement.
Oak-aged apple brandy from Normandy, sometimes with pear.
Aquavit styles.
Caraway- or dill-led aquavit without an aged style designation.
Unaged aquavit led by caraway or dill.
Barrel-aged aquavit, kept distinct from unaged aquavit in recipes.
Barrel-aged aquavit, such as Linie.
Anise-flavored spirits used for pours and rinses.
Absinthe; follow the recipe amount, including when used as a rinse.
Pastis for recipes that specify it.
Sweeter French anise spirit, such as Ricard, lower in strength than absinthe.
Fruit-flavored liqueurs.
Orange liqueur; refine to a specific style or bottle when the recipe needs it.
Orange liqueurs including triple sec, curaçao, and brandy- or rum-based styles. Bottles share this broad recipe role; link a specific bottle when needed.
Orange liqueurs including triple sec, curaçao, and brandy- or rum-based styles, such as Cointreau and Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao. Link a specific bottle when a recipe names one.

Orange liqueur of any style, for recipes that just say orange liqueur. Its subtypes Curaçao, Triple Sec, and Blue Curaçao are for recipes that name one; link a specific bottle when a recipe names one.
Maraschino liqueur, distinct from cherry brandy and cherry syrup.
Cherry liqueur for recipes that specify it.
Sweet cherry liqueur, such as Cherry Heering, distinct from Maraschino Liqueur and kirsch.
Apricot liqueur, distinct from dry apricot brandy.
Sweet apricot liqueur, such as Marie Brizard Apry or Giffard Abricot du Roussillon. Classic recipes call it apricot brandy; an unsweetened apricot eau de vie such as barack pálinka is something else.
Sweet peach-flavored liqueur; distinguish from unsweetened peach brandy.
Sweet peach-flavored liqueur, also called crème de pêche; distinguish from unsweetened peach brandy.
Blackcurrant liqueur, including creme de cassis.
Blackcurrant liqueur, such as crème de cassis.
Sweet banana-flavored liqueur used as a cocktail modifier.
Sweet banana-flavored liqueur used as a cocktail modifier, such as crème de banane.
Herbal liqueurs; select a type or bottle when the recipe specifies a particular profile.
Green herbal liqueur; use a specific bottle reference when a particular bottling is intended.
Green herbal liqueur; link a specific bottle when the recipe names one.
Strong, intensely herbal green liqueur in the style of Green Chartreuse. Link a specific bottle when a recipe names one.
Yellow herbal liqueur; use a specific bottle reference when needed.
Sweeter, milder yellow herbal liqueur in the style of Yellow Chartreuse. Link a specific bottle when a recipe names one.
A sweet herbal and spiced liqueur; link a bottle for the specific bottling you own.
A sweet herbal and spiced liqueur; add a bottle to record what you own.
Flower-flavored liqueurs used as cocktail modifiers.
Sweet floral liqueur flavored with elderflower.
Sweet violet-flavored floral liqueur, also called creme de violette.
Sweet violet-flavored floral liqueur, also called crème de violette.
Spice-led liqueurs; each type retains its distinct recipe role.
Allspice liqueur, also called pimento dram.
Falernum; sweetness and alcohol content vary between preparations and bottlings.
Falernum liqueur, distinct from nonalcoholic Falernum Syrup. Sweetness and strength vary by bottling.
Falernum liqueur, distinct from nonalcoholic Falernum Syrup. Sweetness and strength vary by bottle.
Falernum liqueur, distinct from non-alcoholic Falernum Syrup. Sweetness and strength vary by bottle.
Bitter liqueurs grouped as amaro for cocktail browsing. Styles vary in sweetness, strength, and bitterness; choose a type or bottle when it matters.
Red bitter liqueur; specify a bottle where bitterness and sweetness matter.
Campari-style bitter liqueur, distinct from the Aperol-style Orange Bitter Liqueur recipe role. Color alone does not determine membership.
Bitter red aperitivo liqueur in the style of Campari. Lighter, sweeter aperitivos like Aperol are Orange Bitter Liqueur.
Bitter liqueur with gentian character; select a bottle to capture the specific formulation.
Bitter liqueurs in the gentian recipe role, including Salers, Suze, Avèze, and, in this cabinet, Bitter Bianco. Formulations and strengths vary; select a bottle when needed.
Bitter gentian-root liqueurs, such as Salers, Suze, and Avèze. Formulations and strengths vary; link a bottle when a recipe names one.
A strongly bitter herbal liqueur in the fernet style.
Intensely bitter, minty herbal liqueur, such as Fernet-Branca.
A bitter herbal liqueur in an artichoke-based style.
Bitter herbal amaro made with artichoke, such as Cynar.
Nut-flavored liqueurs. Add other nut styles when useful to your recipes.
Liqueurs that taste nutty, such as amaretto, crème de noyaux, Frangelico (hazelnut), and nocino (walnut). Go by taste: amaretto and crème de noyaux taste of almond even when made from apricot pits.
Sweet almond-flavored liqueur in the amaretto style.
Sweet coffee-flavored liqueur; sugar content and strength vary by bottling.
Sweet coffee-flavored liqueur; sugar content and strength vary by bottle.
Chocolate liqueur; specify light or dark when the recipe needs that distinction.

Still white wine in a dry style, used as a cocktail ingredient.
Red wine, including when used as a float.
Sparkling wines used to lengthen cocktails.
Dry sparkling wine when no narrower style is specified.
Sparkling wine from Champagne; record the specific bottling when its style matters.
Sparkling wine from Champagne; record the specific bottle when its style matters.
Prosecco; sweetness varies by bottling.
Prosecco; sweetness varies by bottle.

Vermouth styles: sweet, dry, blanc, and bitter.
Sweet aromatized fortified wine for recipes calling for sweet vermouth.
Dry aromatized fortified wine for recipes calling for dry vermouth.
Sweet white vermouth, also called bianco or blanc.

Dry sherry in the fino style.
Dry sherry in the amontillado style.
Sherry in the oloroso style; use the sweetness specified by your recipe.
Sweet Pedro Ximénez sherry.

Fortified wine in the ruby port style.
Young, fruity red port, aged briefly in large vats.
Fortified wine in the tawny port style.
Red port aged longer in small casks, nutty and caramel-toned.
Quinine-flavored aperitif wine; use a bottle reference for a particular formulation.

Concentrated aromatic bitters used in dashes or other small seasoning amounts.

Creole-style aromatic bitters for recipes that specify that profile.
Bright red, anise-forward aromatic bitters in the style of Peychaud’s.
Concentrated chocolate-flavored bitters used as cocktail seasoning.

Pineapple juice, fresh by default.

Sugar and water syrups with a defined ratio by weight.
Syrups made from sugar, honey, or agave without added flavorings. Record dilution and concentration on the ingredient page; flavor from the sweetener itself does not make a syrup flavored.
White sugar and water at 1:1 by weight. Nominal Brix: 50.
preparation:
Combine equal weights of white sugar and water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. The listed Brix is nominal, not a measurement of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

Combine equal weights of white sugar and water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. Concentration figures are nominal, not measurements of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

description: White sugar and water at 2:1 by weight. Nominal Brix: approximately 66.7.
preparation:
Combine two parts by weight of white sugar and one part by weight of water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. The listed Brix is nominal, not a measurement of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

Combine two parts by weight of white sugar and one part by weight of water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. Concentration figures are nominal, not measurements of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

description: Demerara sugar and water at 2:1 by weight. Nominal sugar concentration: approximately 66.7 percent; actual Brix can vary.
preparation:
Combine two parts by weight of demerara sugar and one part by weight of water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. The listed Brix is nominal, not a measurement of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

Combine two parts by weight of demerara sugar and one part by weight of water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. Concentration figures are nominal, not measurements of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

description: Flavored syrups; recipe details and concentration belong on the ingredient page.
Syrups flavored with fruit, nuts, spices, or other added ingredients. Recipe details and concentration belong on the ingredient page.
Almond syrup; concentration and flavor vary by preparation.
Pomegranate syrup; document the preparation or purchased source you use.
Honey diluted with water. Specify the ratio for your recipes.
Agave-based sweetener. Document whether it is diluted.
A sweet ginger preparation; record the concentration and preparation you use.
A sweet cinnamon preparation; record the concentration and preparation you use.
Sweetened passion fruit syrup, distinct from unsweetened juice.
Carbonated cocktail mixers.
Unflavored carbonated water.
Unflavored carbonated water, also sold as seltzer or sparkling water. Club soda, with added minerals, is its subtype.
Carbonated bitter-sweet mixer; sweetness and flavor vary by brand.
Ginger-flavored mixer used for a more pronounced ginger profile; brands vary.
Ginger-flavored soft drink, kept distinct from ginger beer in recipes.
Ginger soft drink, milder and sweeter than ginger beer.
Cola-flavored soft drink used as a cocktail mixer.
High-fat dairy cream for recipes that specify cream.
Dairy milk for recipes calling for milk; use a separate ingredient where a substitution changes the recipe.
The white of an egg, used for texture and foam in cocktails.
A whole egg, including yolk, for flips and other cocktails that specify it.
Fresh mint leaves or sprigs for flavor and garnish.
Lime peel for garnish or expressed oils.
Lemon peel for garnish or expressed oils.
Orange peel for garnish or expressed oils.
A prepared cherry used as a cocktail garnish.
Salt; keep a saline solution separate when a recipe specifies one.
Aperol-style bitter liqueur, distinct from the Campari-style Red Bitter Liqueur recipe role and from Orange Liqueur. Color alone does not determine membership.
Lighter, sweeter bitter aperitivo in the style of Aperol, at about half Campari’s strength. Not an Orange Liqueur.
Nonalcoholic spiced falernum syrup, distinct from Falernum liqueur. Record the preparation or purchased source you use.
Non-alcoholic spiced falernum syrup, distinct from Falernum liqueur. Record the preparation or purchased source you use.
Sweetened coconut cream used for sweetness and texture in cocktails, distinct from unsweetened coconut cream or coconut milk.
Lightly aged rum filtered to remove color, with a relatively restrained flavor profile; Don Q Cristal is an example. Distinct from White Blended Rum.
Light, clean rum, usually lightly aged and filtered clear, such as Don Q Cristal. A clear blend with more character is White Blended Rum.
Clear multi-region rum blends, such as Probitas, combining different flavor profiles. Components may be aged or unaged; kept distinct from the more restrained Light Rum role.
Clear rum blended from several regions for more character than Light Rum, such as Probitas. Its components may be aged or unaged.

Moderately aged Barbados-style blends of pot- and column-still rum, represented by Real McCoy 5, Planteray Barbados 5 Year, and Mount Gay Eclipse. Older expressions such as Real McCoy 12 generally fit; lighter white styles such as Real McCoy 3 and Mount Gay Silver do not.

Moderately aged Barbados-style blends of pot- and column-still rum, such as Real McCoy 5, Planteray Barbados 5 Year, and Mount Gay Eclipse. Older expressions generally fit too; Barbados white rums do not.

Aged column-still rum in the recipe role represented by Ron Abuelo Añejo and Don Q Gold, kept distinct from Aged Barbados Rum. Moderately aged expressions are typical; older expressions can generally fill the same role.
Aged rum made only in column stills, lighter-bodied than Barbados-style blends, such as Ron Abuelo Añejo and Don Q Gold. Older expressions generally fit too.
High-strength barrel-aged Jamaican rum for recipes specifying this role, distinct from Unaged Overproof Jamaican Rum and standard-strength Aged Jamaican Rum.
High-strength, lightly aged Jamaican rum in the recipe role represented by Smith & Cross. Distinct from Unaged Overproof Jamaican Rum; its bottles also fill recipes calling for Aged Jamaican Rum.
High-strength, lightly aged Jamaican rum, such as Smith & Cross. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Aged Jamaican Rum.
High-strength unaged Jamaican rum for recipes specifying this role, distinct from Aged Overproof Jamaican Rum.
High-strength unaged Jamaican rum, such as Wray & Nephew White Overproof. Not a substitute for Aged Overproof Jamaican Rum.
Demerara rum bottled at 151 US proof (75.5% ABV), for recipes specifying this strength and style. Distinct from standard-strength Demerara Rum and multi-region overproof blends.
Demerara rum bottled at 151 US proof (75.5% ABV), such as Hamilton 151. Standard-strength Demerara Rum and overproof blends are separate types.
High-strength rum blends, including O.F.T.D., Hamilton Zombie Blend, and Planteray Mister Fogg. Their strengths and flavor profiles differ; recipes often specify a particular bottle.
Unaged sugarcane-juice rhum in the agricole style, also called rhum agricole blanc. Kept distinct from Aged Rhum Agricole.
Unaged rhum agricole (rhum agricole blanc), distilled from fresh sugarcane juice.

Traditional Barbancourt-style white rum without wood maturation; steel-tank resting is compatible with this type. Keep distinct from Aged Haitian Rum and Clairin. Preserve a recipe’s named bottle and strength.
Barrel-aged Haitian rum in the Barbancourt-style recipe role, represented by Barbancourt 3 Star and 5 Star. Keep distinct from Unaged Haitian Rum and Clairin.

Unaged Mexican cane-juice rum in the recipe role represented by Paranubes Blanco, with pronounced fermentation and savory character. Choose other bottles for their fit with this profile; recipes may specify a particular bottle or strength.
Jamaican rum with pronounced caramel influence, distinct from the Aged Jamaican Rum recipe role. Color alone does not determine membership.
Dark, molasses-rich Jamaican rum, such as Coruba or Myers’s, for recipes that want its weight rather than an aged rum. A dark color alone doesn’t make a rum this type.
Pineapple-flavored rum, including Stiggins’ Fancy. Other pineapple rums can differ substantially in flavor; recipes often name the intended bottle.

Gin with prominent citrus, floral, herbal, or other botanical notes, in a recipe role distinct from London Dry Gin. Individual gins can differ substantially; preserve a recipe’s named bottle when specified.
Gin led by citrus, floral, herbal, or other botanicals rather than juniper, such as Hendrick’s or Aviation. These gins differ a lot, so keep a recipe’s named bottle.
Apple brandy and applejack styles used in recipes. A family reference can use any of these types; the Apple Brandy type means regular apple brandy.
Sweet mint liqueur, including clear expressions such as Menthe-Pastille. Kept distinct from the Green Herbal Liqueur recipe role; color alone does not determine membership.
Sweet mint liqueur, green or clear, such as Tempus Fugit or Menthe-Pastille. Green herbal liqueurs are a separate type.
Bitter liqueurs grouped as amaro for cocktail browsing. Includes the Amaro type and specialized styles; choose a type or bottle when the recipe requires one.

A general amaro ingredient type for bottles such as Averna, Montenegro, Meletti, Lucano, and Nonino. Their flavor profiles, sweetness, and strengths differ; use a specific bottle reference when a recipe names one. Use the specialized types for red or orange bitter liqueurs, gentian liqueurs, fernet, and artichoke amaro.

Catch-all for amari without a more specific type, such as Averna, Montenegro, Meletti, Lucano, and Nonino. Their flavor, sweetness, and strength differ, so they are likely substitutes rather than interchangeable: recipes usually name the bottle. Use the specialized types for red or orange bitter liqueurs, gentian liqueurs, fernet, and artichoke amaro.
Bitter vermouth in the recipe role represented by Punt e Mes and Cocchi Dopo Teatro, kept distinct from ordinary Sweet Vermouth. Preserve a recipe’s named bottle when specified.
Sweet vermouth with a pronounced bitter edge, such as Punt e Mes and Cocchi Dopo Teatro. Keep a recipe’s named bottle.
Vanilla-flavored sugar syrup. Record the preparation and sugar concentration you use; vanilla extracts and liqueurs are different ingredients.
Angostura aromatic bitters. Recipes can name this bottle specifically or call for its Aromatic Bitters type. Set availability or quantities to record your stock.
Catch-all for flavored rums without close substitutes, such as coconut rums. Bottles in this type are rarely interchangeable, so recipes usually name the bottle. Pineapple Rum has its own type.

Catch-all for flavored rums without close substitutes, such as coconut rums. Bottles in this type are rarely interchangeable, so recipes usually name the bottle. Pineapple Rum and Spiced Rum have their own types.
Sweet pineapple liqueur, distinct from pineapple-flavored rum.
Sweet melon liqueur, such as Midori.
Bergamot-orange liqueur, such as Italicus, distinct from the broader Orange Liqueur role.
Bergamot-orange liqueur, such as Italicus; more floral and bitter than Orange Liqueur.
Herbal and spice-led liqueurs, in one family because many products sit on the boundary between the two. Select a type or bottle when the recipe specifies a particular profile.
Catch-all for herbal liqueurs without close substitutes, such as Bénédictine, Becherovka, and Chareau. Bottles in this type are rarely interchangeable, so recipes usually name the bottle.
Vanilla-forward liqueurs such as Licor 43 and Galliano, often with citrus or other spice notes. Close enough to substitute in many recipes.

Vanilla liqueurs such as Giffard Vanille de Madagascar and Drillaud, as well as richer vanilla-led liqueurs such as Galliano and Licor 43 that add citrus, herbal, or spice notes. Close enough to substitute in many recipes.
Catch-all for spice-led liqueurs without close substitutes, such as chai spice liqueurs. Bottles in this type are rarely interchangeable, so recipes usually name the bottle.

Catch-all for spice-led liqueurs without close substitutes, such as chai liqueurs, Ancho Reyes chile liqueur, or ginger liqueurs like Domaine de Canton. Bottles in this type are rarely interchangeable, so recipes usually name the bottle.
Aromatized wine aperitifs outside the vermouth styles.
Quinquina-style aromatized wine, such as Cocchi Americano and Lillet Blanc, with quinine or other bitter notes. Kept distinct from Blanc Vermouth.
Quinquina-style aromatized wine with quinine or other bitter notes, such as Cocchi Americano and Lillet Blanc.
Concentrated grapefruit-flavored bitters used as cocktail seasoning.
Spiced bitters in the tiki style, such as Bittermens ‘Elemakule; profiles vary by brand.
Catch-all for one-of-a-kind bitters without close substitutes. Recipes usually name the bottle; use a flavor type such as Aromatic or Orange Bitters when one fits.
Salt for rims and seasoning. Saline Solution is its own note.
20% saline: 20 g salt dissolved in 80 g water. Another strength is its own staple, such as Saline Solution (25%).
Fresh mint leaves or sprigs for flavor and garnish.
Still water, for recipes that call for it.
High-fat dairy cream for recipes that specify cream.
Dairy milk for recipes calling for milk. Add a separate staple where a substitution changes the recipe.
Whole cinnamon sticks for garnish and infusions.
Whole nutmeg to grate over a drink.
Eggs for whites and whole-egg drinks. Set availability when you buy them.
Bottled-in-bond bourbon, at 100 US proof (50% ABV), for recipes calling for bonded bourbon. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Bourbon.
Bottled-in-bond rye whiskey, at 100 US proof (50% ABV), for recipes calling for bonded rye. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Rye Whiskey.
Spirits distilled from fruit: grape brandy, apple brandy, and unaged fruit brandies such as kirsch and pisco.

Aged grape brandy, what a recipe means by plain brandy. Cognac and Armagnac are its subtypes, so their bottles fill these recipes too. Other French, Spanish, and American grape brandies go here. Unaged grape brandy such as pisco is not this type.
Unsweetened cherry eau de vie (kirschwasser), distinct from cherry liqueur and Maraschino Liqueur.
Light Canadian whisky, usually a corn-based blend, such as Canadian Club; Canadians often call it rye. Rye Whiskey is a separate type.
Japanese whisky, most often a light blend for highballs, such as Suntory Toki. Not a substitute for Scotch in recipes that name it.
Rum flavored with vanilla, cinnamon, clove, and other spices, such as Sailor Jerry or Kraken. Sweetness and strength vary, but recipes calling for spiced rum treat bottles as interchangeable.
Vodka, plain or flavored. Add a type here for each flavored vodka you buy.
Liqueurs made with cream or egg, such as Irish cream, RumChata, Amarula, and advocaat. They curdle with citrus and keep best refrigerated once opened.
Irish whiskey and cream liqueur, such as Baileys.
Liqueurs that aren’t fruit, herbal or spice, floral, nut, bitter, or cream: coffee, chocolate, and other flavors such as corn (Nixta), honey, maple, butterscotch, or tea.
Port styles. A recipe calling for plain port accepts any of them.
Port from white grapes, dry to sweet, as in a Portonic with tonic water.
Peychaud’s bitters, the anise-forward bitters of the Sazerac. Recipes can name this bottle specifically or call for its Creole Bitters type. Set availability or quantities to record your stock.
White granulated sugar, for rims and for recipes that call for sugar itself rather than a syrup.
White sugar cubes, for an Old Fashioned or Champagne Cocktail built on a cube.
Freshly pulled espresso; cold brew concentrate is a different staple.
Worcestershire sauce, for savory drinks such as the Bloody Mary.
Vinegar-based hot sauce, such as Tabasco. Recipes naming a specific sauce can link it as its own staple.
Soda water with added minerals, such as sodium bicarbonate, for a slightly salty taste. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Soda Water; plain soda water is offered as a substitute for it.
Grapefruit peel for garnish or expressed oils.

Orange liqueur on a brandy or rum base, richer than triple sec, such as Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao, Senior Curaçao of Curaçao, Grand Marnier, and Clément Créole Shrubb. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Orange Liqueur.
Orange liqueur on a neutral spirit base, clean and dry, such as Cointreau and Combier. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Orange Liqueur.
Orange liqueur colored blue, usually on a neutral base and sweeter than triple sec, such as Bols and Giffard. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Orange Liqueur.
Sweet blackcurrant liqueur, the liqueur of the Kir and El Diablo.
Sweet blackberry liqueur, such as crème de mûre, the liqueur of the Bramble. Liqueurs from blackberry cultivars such as marionberry fit here too.
Sweet violet-flavored floral liqueur, the liqueur of the Aviation. Crème Yvette, with berries and vanilla, is a bottle of its own.

Rich syrup of less-refined cane sugar, rounder and a little grassier than white-sugar rich simple, such as Petite Canne. Its bottles also fill recipes calling for Simple Syrup (2:1). Louisiana cane syrup, such as Steen’s, is boiled cane juice, dark like molasses, and not this.
preparation:
Combine two parts by weight of cane sugar and one part by weight of water. This ratio is by weight. Stir until dissolved. Concentration figures are nominal, not measurements of a prepared batch.

Reference: [Simple syrup ratios and Brix](https://www.cocktailarium.com/lessons/sweetness-i-simple-syrup).

description: Lillet Blanc, the aperitif wine of the Vesper, Corpse Reviver No. 2, and Twentieth Century. Since 1986 it has been less bitter than the Kina Lillet older recipes were written for, which is why many bartenders use Cocchi Americano instead: link the type when any bottle of it will do. Set availability or quantities to record your stock.

Very dark rum with blackstrap molasses added after distilling, bitter and burnt-sugar rich with little aging, such as Cruzan Black Strap. A disputed category, kept because recipes such as the modern Jungle Bird call for it. Not Black Jamaican Rum, whose weight is Jamaican character and caramel.

Alpine liqueur of génépi artemisia from Savoie and the Aosta Valley, herbal, floral, and lightly bitter, such as Dolin Génépy le Chamois. Lighter and less sweet than Green Herbal Liqueur, and without absinthe’s anise.
Sweetened raspberry syrup, homemade or bottled, as in the Clover Club.
Sweetened strawberry syrup, homemade or bottled.
Sweetened pineapple syrup, homemade or bottled. Gum (gomme) syrup, thickened with gum arabic for a silkier texture, counts too: recipes treat them as interchangeable.
Sweetened, preserved lime, homemade or bottled such as Rose’s, the original Gimlet ingredient. Not a stand-in for fresh Lime Juice, nor the other way round.
Unsweetened pear eau de vie, usually from Williams (Bartlett) pears, such as Clear Creek Pear Brandy; distinct from Pear Liqueur.

Sweet pear liqueur, on a neutral, brandy, or cognac base, such as Mathilde Poire, Rothman & Winter Orchard Pear, and Belle de Brillet. Spiced pear liqueur is its own type: the spice changes too much to fill these recipes. Distinct from unsweetened Pear Brandy.
Lemon-flavored vodka, such as Absolut Citron, the vodka of the Cosmopolitan.
Vanilla-flavored vodka, the vodka of the Porn Star Martini.

Catch-all for flavored vodkas without close substitutes, such as pepper or berry vodkas. Bottles in this type are rarely interchangeable, so recipes usually name the bottle. Citron Vodka and Vanilla Vodka have their own types.
